Methodology

Overview

This dashboard estimates the causal impact of the Iran war crisis (onset February 28, 2026) on global shipping and trade flows. For each series (chokepoint, regional port group, country aggregate, or individual port), a counterfactual path is constructed representing what traffic would have looked like absent the crisis. The deviation between the actual observed data and the counterfactual is attributed to the crisis.

Data comes from IMF PortWatch, which aggregates AIS (Automatic Identification System) satellite vessel tracking data. Daily counts and capacity (deadweight tonnage) for five vessel types (tanker, container, dry bulk, general cargo, and RoRo) are aggregated to weekly frequency to smooth day-of-week effects while preserving timely signal. Weeks run Monday through Sunday, with each week labeled by its Monday start date. Within each week, values represent the daily average (not the sum), and incomplete trailing weeks (fewer than 5 days of data) are dropped to avoid partial-week distortions.

A clean resampling boundary is enforced at the crisis date: pre-crisis and post-crisis daily data are resampled to weekly frequency independently, ensuring no week blends pre- and post-crisis days. If the first post-crisis week is a short stub (crisis onset mid-week), it is merged into the following full week to avoid a noisy partial bin.

Counterfactual Construction (Multiplicative via Log-Space STL)

The decomposition is estimated in log space to ensure counterfactuals are always non-negative (trade flows cannot be negative). Each series is first transformed via log1p(x), then STL is applied additively in log space, and the counterfactual is converted back via expm1(). This is equivalent to a multiplicative model in level space:

counterfactual(t) = expm1( trend(t) + seasonal(t) + predicted_remainder(t) )

The log1p/expm1 pair handles zeros gracefully (log1p(0) = 0, expm1(0) = 0). Log-space is applied when all values are non-negative and at least 10% of the series is strictly positive. A final clip(lower=0) is applied as a hard floor.

Step 1: STL Decomposition

Each log-transformed weekly series is decomposed using STL (Seasonal-Trend decomposition using LOESS) with period=52 (annual seasonality), seasonal=13 (quarterly-scale seasonal smoothing window), and robust=True to downweight outliers. The seasonal smoother at s=13 is responsive enough to capture evolving seasonal patterns without overfitting year-to-year noise.

Critically, the STL is estimated on pre-crisis data only (June 2019 through February 27, 2026) to prevent the crisis-period collapse from contaminating the seasonal and trend estimates. Post-crisis seasonal values are projected forward using a seasonal week-lookup table: for each ISO calendar week, the table stores the average of that week’s seasonal values from the most recent 3 years of pre-crisis data. This raw lookup is then smoothed with a 5-week circular moving average (half-window=2, wrapping around the 52-week boundary) to prevent implausible week-on-week spikes in the counterfactual caused by STL seasonal overfitting to individual years.

This produces three components (all in log space):

  • Trend: The slow-moving structural level of the series (e.g., gradual growth in Hormuz traffic as Asian demand rises, or the step-down in Bab el-Mandeb after the 2024 Houthi disruption).
  • Seasonal: The repeating annual cycle (e.g., higher tanker traffic in winter months due to heating oil demand, lower in spring shoulder season).
  • Remainder: Everything left over — short-run fluctuations driven by economic conditions, oil market dynamics, weather events, and noise.

Step 2: Trend Extrapolation

To project the trend into the post-crisis period, a linear regression (np.polyfit, degree 1) is fitted to the last 13 weeks of pre-crisis trend values in log space. This captures the recent trajectory (rising, falling, or flat) and extends it forward at the same slope. The 13-week window balances responsiveness to recent shifts against stability. For the short post-crisis horizons here (~4 weeks), the choice of extrapolation method has minimal impact.

Step 3: Seasonal Projection

The smoothed seasonal week-lookup table (described in Step 1) maps each post-crisis calendar week to its expected seasonal value in log space. Because the lookup is built from a 3-year average and then smoothed with a 5-week circular moving average, week-to-week transitions are gentle and the counterfactual avoids jagged seasonal artifacts.

Step 4: Remainder Prediction (RidgeCV + AR Lags + Fourier Harmonics + Geographic Cross-Features)

After removing trend and seasonal, the leftover remainder captures short-run dynamics. A RidgeCV regression (leave-one-out cross-validation over alphas [0.01, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 5, 10, 50, 100], R² scoring, features standardized to zero mean and unit variance) is fitted on the pre-crisis training window to predict the remainder from five groups of features:

  • Frozen monthly macro controls (14): Gulf/Hormuz oil production, OPEC total production, world petroleum production (all EIA); US industrial production; US capacity utilization; vehicle sales; commercial & industrial loans; IMF energy price index; IMF non-fuel commodity index; China imports; China exports; consumer sentiment; retail sales; and Global Economic Policy Uncertainty (EPU) index. All forward-filled to weekly frequency and frozen at their last pre-crisis values.
  • Frozen daily/weekly controls (8): USD broad index, federal funds rate, US EPU, 10-year breakeven inflation, VIX, yield curve (10Y−2Y), 4-week average initial jobless claims, and weekly gasoline supplied. Averaged to weekly frequency and frozen at last pre-crisis values.
  • Fourier harmonics (6 features): Sine/cosine pairs at annual (52-week), semi-annual (26-week), and quarterly (13-week) periods, computed as sin/cos(2π × day_of_year / period_days). These deterministic calendar features give the remainder model a second chance to capture sub-annual periodicities that the single STL seasonal pass may miss (e.g., quarterly contract-timing cycles, semi-annual refinery turnaround schedules).
  • AR(2) lags (2 features): The remainder’s own values at lag-1 and lag-2, capturing week-to-week momentum (autocorrelation) in the residual. Frozen at their last pre-crisis values post-crisis.
  • Geographic cross-features (0–6 features): STL remainder of upstream “feeder” chokepoints, both contemporaneous (t) and lagged (t−1). These capture the propagation of shipping flow shocks through the global network. For example, the Strait of Hormuz remainder is used as a predictor for Suez Canal, Cape of Good Hope, and downstream Asian ports; the Malacca Strait remainder feeds into Singapore, East Asian, and Southeast Asian models. A geographic linkage map defines which chokepoints inform each target (up to 3 feeders × 2 lags = up to 6 cross-features). Like AR lags, all cross-features are frozen at their last pre-crisis values to prevent crisis-period contamination. See “Geographic Cross-Series Features” below for details.

Total feature count per model: ~30–36 (14 monthly + 8 daily + 6 Fourier + 2 AR lags + 0–6 geographic cross-features). A minimum of 20 pre-crisis observations is required for the Ridge regression to be fitted.

Step 5: Freezing Controls Post-Crisis

The central design choice: all control variables, AR lags, and geographic cross-features are frozen at their last pre-crisis values when projecting the counterfactual forward. This means the counterfactual answers “what would have happened if economic conditions and shipping momentum had continued as they were immediately before the crisis?” Without freezing, crisis-period shocks (collapsing tanker counts, surging oil prices) would feed back through the AR lags and live controls into the counterfactual, shrinking the estimated deviation toward zero.

The sensitivity model relaxes this for a subset of daily financial variables, allowing Brent crude, WTI, Henry Hub natural gas, high-yield credit spreads, and BDRY/FRO shipping indices to update live. This captures an alternative scenario where financial market movements since the crisis would have affected shipping volumes even absent the physical disruption.

Geographic Cross-Series Features

Global shipping flows are interconnected: a disruption at one chokepoint propagates downstream through the network. To capture this, the pipeline uses a two-pass architecture. In the first pass, STL decomposition is run on all 28 chokepoints and the total_count remainder is stored. In the second pass, when fitting the Ridge model for any target series (chokepoint, region, country, or individual port), the remainders of geographically upstream “feeder” chokepoints are included as additional predictors.

The geographic linkage map encodes domain knowledge about shipping network topology:

  • Persian Gulf & Indian Ocean chain: Hormuz → Bab el-Mandeb → Suez/Cape
  • Asian trade routes: Hormuz + Malacca → East Asia, Southeast Asia, Indian Subcontinent
  • European routes: Suez + Gibraltar → Mediterranean, Dover → Northwest Europe
  • Americas: Panama + Yucatan → North America, Panama + Magellan → Latin America
  • Chokepoint-to-chokepoint: e.g., Malacca feeds Taiwan Strait, Korea Strait, Lombok, Sunda, Makassar

For each feeder, two features are added: the contemporaneous remainder (at time t) and the 1-week lag (t−1). Both are frozen at their last pre-crisis values post-crisis, identical to the AR lag treatment. Country-level models use the same map via ISO3 codes (e.g., CHN → Malacca + Taiwan Strait + Korea Strait).

In A/B testing, adding cross-features improved the controls R² in 96% of series across regions and countries, with a mean ΔR² of +0.08. The largest gains were in downstream regions furthest from the crisis origin (Northwest Europe: +0.35, East Asia: +0.25), where intermediary chokepoint flows carry the strongest propagation signal.

Deviation Calculation

The “deviation” reported throughout this dashboard measures the percentage gap between what actually happened and what the model predicts would have happened absent the crisis. The formula depends on the counterfactual value:

  • If counterfactual > 0: deviation = (actual − counterfactual) / counterfactual × 100%
  • If counterfactual ≤ 0 but pre-crisis average > 0: deviation = (actual − counterfactual) / pre_crisis_avg × 100%
  • Otherwise: deviation = 0 (no meaningful baseline)

The “pre-crisis average” (pre_crisis_avg) is defined as the mean weekly value over the 52 weeks immediately preceding the crisis onset. If fewer than 52 pre-crisis weeks are available, the full pre-crisis mean is used instead.

A deviation of −20% means the observed value is 20% below the counterfactual — i.e., 20% of expected activity is “missing” and attributed to the crisis. A positive deviation means activity exceeded the no-crisis baseline (e.g., rerouted cargo arriving at alternative ports). All deviations are capped at ±999% to prevent extreme values from distorting comparisons.

All deviation figures in the summary tables and KPI cards refer to the most recent complete week of data, not an average over the full post-crisis period. This ensures the dashboard reflects the current state of disruption rather than being diluted by the crisis onset period (when ships already loaded or in transit could distort the picture). The time series charts show the full weekly trajectory for readers who want to see the evolution.

Deviations are computed separately for each of five vessel types: tanker, container, dry bulk, general cargo, and RoRo. The vessel type toggle at the top of the dashboard controls which type is displayed; selecting multiple types shows aggregated port call results where actual and counterfactual values are summed across selected types before computing the deviation percentage. Capacity (deadweight tonnage) is used for chokepoint metrics; import/export tonnage is used for regional port groups.

Map Marker Filtering

The global deviation map suppresses markers for chokepoint×vessel-type combinations with negligible baseline traffic to prevent misleading extreme-percentage markers. Specifically:

  • Capacity markers: Suppressed if the pre-crisis average weekly capacity is below 1,000 deadweight tonnes (e.g., RoRo capacity through the Bering Strait).
  • Ship count markers: Suppressed if the pre-crisis average weekly count is below 2 ships (e.g., container vessels through the Ombai Strait).
  • Port markers: Suppressed if the pre-crisis average weekly tonnage is below 1,000 tonnes.

When a vessel type has negligible traffic at a chokepoint, the multi-vessel-type aggregation treats it as zero (both actual and counterfactual), so it does not pollute the combined deviation for that location. This filtering only affects map markers — the KPI summary cards and detail tables continue to show all series.

Multi-Vessel-Type Port Aggregation

When multiple vessel types are selected, the dashboard aggregates port call data across those types. Each port’s per-vessel-type modeled series (actual and counterfactual) is held separately; the aggregation sums actual values and counterfactual values across the selected types, then computes deviation as (sum_actual − sum_cf) / |sum_cf| × 100%.

Port-level models are initially run for the top 50 ports by volume for each vessel type independently. However, a port may rank in the top 50 for some vessel types but not others (e.g., Singapore is a top-50 tanker port but not a top-50 dry bulk port). To ensure accurate multi-type aggregation, the pipeline runs a second pass that models all missing port×vessel-type combinations using a tiered approach:

  • STL + Ridge (primary): If the port’s weekly series for the missing vessel type has ≥104 weeks of data with ≥30% non-zero values, the full STL decomposition and Ridge regression pipeline is applied, identical to the top-50 methodology.
  • Naive baseline (fallback): If the series is too short or sparse for STL, a naive calendar-week-average baseline is used as the counterfactual, with the deviation normalized by the pre-crisis mean.
  • Pre-crisis average (last resort): If neither STL nor naive is viable (e.g., fewer than 10 pre-crisis weeks of data), the pre-crisis weekly average is used as a flat counterfactual.

This ensures that when you select all five vessel types, every port’s total portcall count includes contributions from all vessel types it serves — not just the types where it ranked in the top 50.

Naive Baseline & YoY/QoQ Comparisons

As a robustness check, a simple naive baseline is also computed for each series. It uses the average of the same ISO calendar weeks from 2023 onward as the counterfactual, and normalizes the deviation by the pre-crisis mean to avoid division-by-zero issues in sparse series.

The detail tables also include two additional naive comparisons: vs 1Y ago (year-over-year, comparing the latest week to the value 52 weeks earlier) and vs 1Q ago (quarter-over-quarter, 13 weeks earlier). These simple look-back comparisons provide context independent of any model.

Signal-to-Noise Dimming

Not all deviations shown on the dashboard are statistically meaningful. Some series have high pre-crisis residual variance, meaning the model’s fit is noisy and a large-looking deviation may fall within the range of normal fluctuation. To help distinguish genuine crisis signals from noise, the dashboard dims values that do not pass a significance threshold.

How it works: For each series, the standard deviation (σ) of the pre-crisis residuals (percentage deviations between actual and counterfactual during the training window) is computed. A deviation is considered significant if |deviation| ≥ tσ, where t is the threshold set by the Noise filter slider in the info bar. Values below this threshold are displayed at reduced opacity (dimmed) in both the KPI summary cards and detail tables.

Interactive threshold: The slider ranges from 0σ to 4σ in steps of 0.5, defaulting to 2σ. At 2σ, roughly the top 5% of pre-crisis fluctuations would exceed the threshold under a normal distribution. Lower values (e.g. 1σ) show more values as significant; higher values (e.g. 3σ) are stricter and dim more aggressively. Setting the slider to 0 disables dimming entirely, showing all deviations at full opacity. Changes apply instantly to both the pre-rendered single-vessel panels and the dynamically aggregated multi-vessel panels.

Multi-vessel-type mode: When multiple vessel types are selected, the dashboard aggregates actual and counterfactual values across the selected types before computing the deviation. The significance test, however, is applied per vessel type individually. A metric is dimmed in multi-vessel mode only if all selected vessel types are below the tσ threshold for that metric. If any single vessel type shows a significant deviation, the aggregated value remains fully visible, since the signal from that vessel type is considered meaningful even if other types are noisy.

Edge cases: Series with fewer than 20 pre-crisis observations, or where the pre-crisis residual standard deviation is near zero (<0.01%), default to significant (undimmed), since there is insufficient history to estimate the noise band.

Regional Aggregates vs. Per-Port Estimates

The dashboard presents two levels of port analysis that are estimated independently and should not be expected to be arithmetically consistent. Regional port group aggregates (e.g., “East Asian Imports”) sum all daily activity across every port in the region, then run a single STL decomposition and Ridge regression on that aggregate series. Per-port deviations run STL and Ridge independently on each individual port’s weekly series — each port gets its own trend, seasonal pattern, and remainder regression. Summing the per-port counterfactuals would not reproduce the regional aggregate counterfactual because STL decomposition is nonlinear (the trend of a sum is not the sum of the trends). Additionally, the per-port tables show only the top ports by volume, omitting the long tail of smaller ports that are included in the aggregate. The two levels answer different questions: the aggregate captures total regional disruption, while the per-port breakdown identifies which individual ports are most affected.

Data Sources

  • Vessel tracking: IMF PortWatch (AIS satellite data), daily vessel counts and capacity for 28 chokepoints and ~2,000 ports globally, covering five vessel types.
  • Frozen monthly controls (14): Gulf/Hormuz oil production, OPEC total production, world petroleum production (EIA); US industrial production; US capacity utilization; vehicle sales; commercial & industrial loans; IMF energy price index; IMF non-fuel commodity index; China imports; China exports; consumer sentiment; retail sales; Global EPU index.
  • Frozen daily/weekly controls (8): USD broad index, federal funds rate, US EPU, 10-year breakeven inflation, VIX, yield curve (10Y−2Y), 4-week average initial jobless claims, weekly gasoline supplied.
  • Live daily controls (sensitivity model only, 6): Brent crude, WTI, Henry Hub natural gas, high-yield credit spread, BDRY shipping index, FRO shipping index.
  • Fourier harmonics (6): Sine/cosine pairs at annual (52-week), semi-annual (26-week), and quarterly (13-week) periods.
  • AR lags (2): Lag-1 and lag-2 of the STL remainder (frozen at last pre-crisis values post-crisis).
  • Geographic cross-features (0–6): STL remainder (total vessel count) from upstream feeder chokepoints, contemporaneous + 1-week lag, frozen post-crisis. Up to 3 feeders per target (× 2 lags = up to 6 cross-features per model).

Key Parameters

  • STL: period=52 weeks (annual), seasonal smoother window s=13 (quarterly), robust=True. Estimated on pre-crisis data only in log space. Seasonal projected forward by ISO-week matching (3-year average), smoothed with 5-week circular moving average (half-window=2, wrapping at week 52→1 boundary).
  • Log-space: log1p(x) applied when all values ≥0 and ≥10% are strictly positive. Counterfactual inverted via expm1() then clamped to ≥0.
  • RidgeCV: Alpha selected per series via leave-one-out cross-validation (candidates: 0.01, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 5, 10, 50, 100; R² scoring). ~30–36 features (14 monthly + 8 daily + 6 Fourier + 2 AR + 0–6 cross), standardized (zero mean, unit variance). Minimum 20 training observations required.
  • Trend extrapolation: 13-week linear fit (degree-1 polynomial) on the log-space trend.
  • AR lags: 2 (frozen at last pre-crisis values post-crisis).
  • Crisis onset: February 28, 2026. Training window: June 2019 (after STL burn-in) through February 27, 2026.
  • Weekly aggregation: Daily average within Monday-to-Sunday weeks, with separate resampling at the crisis boundary to prevent blending pre- and post-crisis days. Weeks labeled by Monday start date. Trailing weeks with fewer than 5 days of data are dropped.
  • Vessel types: Tanker, container, dry bulk, general cargo, and RoRo. Select one for per-metric detail (ship count + capacity/tonnage); select multiple for aggregated port call view.
  • Minimum data: 104 weeks (~2 years) and ≥30% non-zero for STL; 52 pre-crisis weeks for naive baseline; 10 weeks for pre-crisis-average fallback. Minimum 20 observations for Ridge regression.
  • Port fill: Top 50 ports per vessel type receive full STL+Ridge models. Ports appearing in any vessel type’s top-50 list receive modeled counterfactuals for all other vessel types via the STL → naive → pre-crisis-average fallback hierarchy.
  • Deviation cap: ±999%. Map markers additionally filtered by minimum pre-crisis average traffic (capacity ≥1,000 DWT; count ≥2 ships/week; port tonnage ≥1,000).

Model Fit: Variance Decomposition

For each modeled series the pipeline computes a variance decomposition on the pre-crisis training window using sequential R², displayed as a stacked bar beneath each chart. This measures how much of the training-period variance in the log-transformed series is explained at each stage: Trend (R² of trend alone vs. the original series), +Seasonal (R² of trend + STL seasonal), +Controls (R² of the full model including Ridge-predicted remainder from Fourier harmonics, macro controls, AR lags, and geographic cross-features), and Unexplained (1 − full R²). Higher unexplained variance means the counterfactual has wider implicit confidence bands. When multiple vessel types are selected, the bar shows a weighted-average decomposition across vessel types, with weights proportional to each type’s pre-crisis historical average level.

Note: R² statistics cover only series with full STL+Ridge models (variance_decomp available). Port-level series using the naive or pre-crisis-average fallback do not produce a variance decomposition and are excluded from this table.

Fit varies systematically by metric type and aggregation level. Port-call series fit substantially better than tonnage series because tonnage depends on vessel size mix, which introduces high-frequency variance that no trend+seasonal model can explain. Aggregated series (regional, median R²=0.63; country, median 0.47) fit better than individual chokepoint-level metrics (median 0.49) because aggregation smooths idiosyncratic noise. The controls (macro variables, Fourier harmonics, AR lags, and geographic cross-features) contribute a median of ~5–7pp of marginal R² on top of trend and seasonal components, with the geographic cross-features contributing the largest gains for downstream entities (mean ΔR²=+0.08 for regions and countries).
